name: Majoritarianism
summary: Majoritarianism holds that the majority of the community's adults has the right to decide collective questions, that its claim outweighs claims of superior wisdom, and that the power to decide should not be limited, divided or entrenched against it. Its institutional form is Lijphart's majoritarian or Westminster model: single-party majority cabinets, a dominant executive, two parties, plurality elections, a unitary state, a flexible constitution and no judicial review. Beyond who decides and how, it states no programme.
scope: The procedural and institutional doctrine of majority rule: Locke's majority-consent argument (Second Treatise, ch. VIII), Kendall's definition of the doctrine of majority rule, Dicey's parliamentary sovereignty and Bagehot's fused executive and legislature, Lijphart's majoritarian (Westminster) model, and Waldron's case against judicial review. It excludes ethnic or religious majoritarianism (a majority defined by identity), and Locke's wider limited-government liberalism, which is not specific to the doctrine.

notes: Searched every theme. The sources are about who decides and by what procedure, so economy, society, culture, ecology and technology are almost wholly null. Lijphart is a critic of the model but describes it as derived from the majority principle, so his list is used for the model's own features. Lijphart's Patterns of Democracy full book, Waldron's Law and Disagreement and Kendall's book were not available as full text; chapters 1-2 and the Yale article were. Dicey's referendum essay (as a check on party majorities) and Bagehot's praise of a revising second chamber point away from pure majoritarianism, so direct votes and second chambers are null. Ethnic or religious majoritarianism is not represented. 2026-11-05 (Brandon): 13 answers resting only on sources that never discuss Majoritarianism (borrowing: Two Treatises of Government; John Locke and the Doctrine of Majority-Rule; Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution; The English Constitution; Democracy) were cleared to null.
